title: Challenge: Indexed Randomized Set

writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only randomized-set program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
The last value now occupies the removed slot. The worked program demonstrates this invariant on an independent fixture, so you can study the implementation before predicting the challenge result.

For teaching input `add1 add2 remove2 add3`, the worked program returns `1,3`. Its functions are complete and use only std. Adapt the same state transitions to the visible challenge input `add4 add9 remove4 add7`; predict that result before opening the answer reveal. The precise contract is: After add 4, add 9, remove 4, add 7, return the dense storage in any valid order shown sorted.

Return canonical output: lowercase booleans, decimal integers without leading zeros, comma-separated values and semicolon-separated groups, with no extra whitespace or final newline. Whole medians use integer form and half medians use .5. Textual sentinels such as none and # retain their stated meaning. String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Solve the exact task, not just the visible example: After add 4, add 9, remove 4, add 7, return the dense storage in any valid order shown sorted. On input `add4 add9 remove4 add7`, predict the output before opening the answer reveal. The revealed output is a test oracle for this case, while private checks exercise other legal cases. Start by stating the input grammar and output format in your own words. Parse the complete input, including surrounding whitespace, before relying on any convenient positions in the example.

Build the solution around one maintained claim: Combine a dense vector with a value-to-index map; delete by swapping with the last item. Decide what state represents that claim, how it is initialized, what a single update does, and when the algorithm stops. A key-derived representation lets later work reuse an earlier fact. It may be a set, a map from keys to state, compressed ranks, or a rolling fingerprint; name which one this pattern uses. Trace the visible input by hand and record at least two intermediate states, not only the final answer. If the trace cannot justify your predicted output, there is a gap between the idea and the implementation.

Check both correctness and cost. The intended bound is O(1) expected per operation · O(n) space; explain which operation dominates it and how many times the input can trigger that operation. Check missing keys, repeated keys, and collisions conceptually; expected constant-time operations are not a worst-case promise. Add one small case that should succeed, one boundary case, and one case chosen to challenge the invariant. Compare your hand result with the program's result, then use a failing case to fix the earliest incorrect state transition rather than patching the final output.
writing.feedback: For this input the result is `8`. The last value now occupies the removed slot. Compare this independent fixture with the worked trace: After adding 4 and 9, removing 4 moves 9 into slot 0. Its map entry must become 9→0. Adding 7 gives dense storage [9,7]; sorting only the final report produces 7,9, without changing the constant-time storage operations.
